country.comment: Study examines special purpose water supply districts in the Houston, Texas metropolitan statistical area (MSA) in the United States under the US Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 2, Introduction; PDF p. 13, Note 1

effect_estimate.comment: In Bayesian joint binomial (any new debt issuance) and gamma (log debt amount issued) multilevel models across 527 water districts (2008–2016; Table A1, PDF p. 17, where minus signs are rendered as '2' in the PDF text layer and verified against Figure 1 and pp. 9–11 text), prior 3-year SDWA health violations alone had no positive unconditional association with new debt issuance (Model 1 log-odds 95% CrI [-0.777, 0.268]; log amount 95% CrI [-0.192, 0.294]), nor did management violations (Model 1 log-odds 95% CrI [-0.220, 0.274]). Higher lagged total tax-and-fee revenue predicted higher log-odds of issuing new debt (Model 1 ln(Revenue_t-1) 95% CrI [0.302, 1.024]), whereas higher lagged fund balance (fiscal slack, US$1m) predicted lower odds of issuing debt overall (Model 1 95% CrI [-0.380, -0.177]) but larger bond amounts when issued (gamma 95% CrI [0.017, 0.091]). Crucially, fiscal slack positively moderated responses to SDWA health violations (Model 3 Fund balance_t-1 * Health violation interaction log-odds 95% CrI [0.153, 0.747]): violating districts with large positive fund balances were significantly more likely to issue new capital debt than compliant districts, whereas violating districts with near-zero or negative fund balances were less likely to issue debt; interactions with ln(Revenue_t-1) (Model 2 95% CrI [-0.215, 1.54]) and median home value (Model 4 95% CrI [-0.113, 0.105]) had 95% CrIs spanning zero.
effect_estimate.value: Across 527 Houston-area water districts (2008–2016), prior 3-year SDWA health violations had no unconditional effect on new capital debt issuance (Model 1 binomial log-odds 95% credible interval [-0.777, 0.268]), while lagged revenue increased debt-issuance log-odds (ln(Revenue_t-1) 95% CrI [0.302, 1.024]) and lagged fund balance reduced overall debt-issuance log-odds (95% CrI [-0.380, -0.177]) but increased bond size given issuance (gamma 95% CrI [0.017, 0.091]). Responding to health violations with new capital debt depended positively on fiscal slack (Model 3 Fund balance_t-1 [US$1m] x Health violation log-odds 95% CrI [0.153, 0.747]), whereas interactions of health violations with ln(Revenue_t-1) (Model 2 95% CrI [-0.215, 1.54]) and median home value (Model 4 95% CrI [-0.113, 0.105]) spanned zero.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 8–11, Results, Figures 1–2; PDF p. 17, Appendix A, Table A1

mechanism_certainty.comment: Observational longitudinal panel study (ceiling <= 2 under CODEBOOK.md §9) documenting statistical associations in administrative datasets (SDWIS, TWDD, TBRB) between regulatory health violations, fragmented special-district fiscal capacity, and new debt issuance, without directly observing internal utility rate-setting, allocation agreements, or credit-market application/refusal processes (PDF p. 10; PDF p. 14, Note 10).
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 5–12, Research design and methods & Results; PDF p. 14, Note 10

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines institutional fragmentation across 527 hyper-localised special purpose water districts (MUDs, WCIDs, FWSDs) whose service-area boundaries tie revenue capacity (property taxes and service fees) and property wealth (census-tract median home values) to local neighbourhoods, inter-entity water purchasing and allocation agreements, and responses to EPA/TCEQ Safe Drinking Water Act health and management violation enforcement.

outcome_flags.comment: Drinking water service quality is directly measured via EPA SDWIS Safe Drinking Water Act health violations (exceeding maximum contaminant/chemical levels or failing mandatory treatment techniques, affecting 3%–5% of districts per year). The regression dependent variable is district-level water infrastructure capital financing (new debt issuance and bond amount), and household tariff/rate structures are explicitly noted as unobserved (PDF p. 14, Note 10).

sample_size.comment: 533 active districts were initially identified in SDWIS in 2016; 3 unmatched to audits and 3 with zero service connections or zero revenue were dropped, yielding 527 districts in the primary sample (with 5 to 9 annual audits observed per district over FY 2008–2016; Note 12). Robustness subsamples examined 478 MUDs (Note 9) and small systems of 476 (<10,000 people) and 222 (<3,300 people) districts (Note 22).
sample_size.value: 527 special purpose public service water districts (478 MUDs, 35 WCIDs, 14 FWSDs) observed across fiscal years 2008–2016 (unbalanced panel)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 6, Data; PDF p. 8, Table 1; PDF pp. 13–15, Notes 9, 12, and 22

study_design.comment: Models yearly district decisions to issue new tax-exempt debt (Bernoulli/logit part) and amount of debt issued conditional on issuance (log-gamma part) from FY 2008 to 2016, using 3-year lagged SDWA violation indicators (2005–2016) and 1-year lagged fiscal indicators, with district and fiscal-year random effects estimated via Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA).
study_design.value: Longitudinal observational panel study (2008–2016) using a two-part semi-continuous cross-classified multilevel hierarchical Bayesian regression model (joint binomial-gamma likelihood estimated via INLA)
study_design.where_found: PDF pp. 5–8, Research design and methods & Results; PDF p. 14, Note 18
